Deriving a model for the whole robot's motion is a bottom-up process

  • Each Wheel
    • Contributes to the robot motion
    • Imposes constraints on the robot's motion
  • Forces and constraints of each wheel must be expressed with respect to a clear and consistent reference frame.

Intro. to Autonomous Robotics08 / 62
Kinematics
Local (robot) reference frame: Three dimensional, describes position on the plane and orientation, {XR,YR,θ}\{X_R, Y_R, \theta\}
Global Reference Frame: Defined by axes XIX_I and YIY_I with some origin O, {XI,YI}\{X_I, Y_I\}
Angular difference between global and reference frames is θ\theta.
Point P on the robot in the global reference frame is specified by coordinates (x,y)(x, y).
Intro. to Autonomous Robotics09 / 62
Kinematics

We can describe the pose (global) as a vector:

ξI=[xyθ]\xi_I = \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ \theta \end{bmatrix}
Intro. to Autonomous Robotics10 / 62
Kinematics

How can we describe the robot motion in terms of component motions?

  • We must first map motion along the axes of the global reference frame along the axes of the robot's local reference frame.
  • This mapping is a function of the current pose of the robot.

Forward kinematics provide an estimate of the robots position given its geometry and speed of its wheels

  • Requires accurate measurement of the wheel velocities over time
  • However, position error (accumulation error) grows over time
  • A differential drive robot with wheels that have speed ϕ˙1\dot{\phi}_1 and ϕ˙2\dot{\phi}_2 has the following forward kinematic model.
